BATCH B · BOARD 4 OF 4

Cold start to first contribution

Screens 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 9, connected. The success condition is not "account created" — it is one artifact in a project and one answer written. Everything between sign-up and that moment is cost, and the annotations below name where we expect to lose people.

← foundation B1 onboarding B2 identity B3 reputation
2PROVIDER CHOICE
DECISION
ORCID · institutional SSO · Google. Three branches, and Google is the weak one.
DROP-OFF RISK · HIGH
The user has no ORCID and cannot find their institution. Mitigation: Google is always available, and the account works unverified — it just cannot post in institutional spaces.
~20 s · A01 A02 A03 R02
3ORCID CONSENT
DECISION
Grant read, and separately decide on write. Write defaults off and nothing downstream depends on it.
DROP-OFF RISK · MEDIUM
A consent screen that reads like a data grab loses cautious researchers here. Mitigation: state what is not requested, and never bundle write with read.
~30 s · A01 A21 N06 N09
4PUBLICATION IMPORT
DECISION · 34 OF THEM
Confirm, reject, merge a duplicate, or say "this isn't me". This is the moment the product feels alive — and the moment it can feel like homework.
DROP-OFF RISK · HIGHEST
34 individual decisions is a wall. Mitigations: "confirm all 31 clean" collapses it to one click, only the 3 ambiguous items demand attention, and Skip for now keeps the list rather than discarding it.
~90 s, or 5 s if skipped · R01 R04 A08
5CO-AUTHORS
DECISION
Follow the 12 who are here; invite up to 5 of the 27 who are not, individually, with the message shown before it sends.
DROP-OFF RISK · LOW, REPUTATION RISK · HIGH
Few people abandon here, but a bulk-blast button would cost us the trust of everyone on the receiving end. The 5-per-week cap is the growth we are willing to buy. "Invite nobody" is a first-class exit.
~40 s · R03 C01 C02 N14
6PERSONA FORK
DECISION · THE BRANCH POINT
PI → create a lab. PhD/Postdoc → ask a question. Industry → set a disclosure floor. Librarian → connect the institution. Four genuinely different next screens.
DROP-OFF RISK · LOW
Cheap to answer. The risk is mis-selection, not abandonment — so the copy says plainly that it sets defaults, never permissions, and is changeable.
~10 s · R06 R08 A04
7CHECKLIST
DECISION
Do the next unlock now, or dismiss the checklist. Three of seven are already done by arriving here.
DROP-OFF RISK · MEDIUM — AND THIS IS WHERE WE LOSE THEM QUIETLY
Nobody rage-quits a checklist; they just close the tab and never come back. Mitigation: the next action is always one action, always time-estimated, and dismissing it locks nothing.
open-ended · K03 K01 R05 R10 B06
9PROFILE, POPULATED
SUCCESS CONDITION
A profile a stranger would trust: verified marker, real outputs, one method card, and a replication axis that is not zero. The flow ends when someone else's work is better off.
WHAT WE MEASURE
Time-to-first-actionable-answer, not time-to-signup. A completed account that never answers anything is a failed onboarding.
day 1 – week 2 · A05 A10 B03 B15
ΣTHE HONEST FUNNEL
Shape, not forecast. We have no traffic yet — these are the relative heights we expect, and the numbers to replace after the pilot.
lands on 2100
consents at 3high
touches import at 4the wall
reaches 6—
first artifactquiet loss
first answer writtenthe real number
The two steps worth engineering hardest are 4 and the gap after 7. Everything else is cheap by comparison.
EVERY STEP IS SKIPPABLE
Screens 4, 5, 6 and 7 all have a real exit that costs the user nothing. A funnel that traps people produces accounts, not contributors — and the metric we care about is on the far side.
NOTHING IS PUBLIC UNTIL STEP 9
Steps 2–7 all carry the PRIVATE chip. The first thing anyone else can see is the profile at step 9, and only after the user has chosen to publish it.
THE MISSING SCREEN
Between 7 and 9 sits the first upload and the first answer — the two acts the flow exists to produce. Neither is in domains A, B or R, so neither is designed yet. They are the first thing the next batch should cover.
